messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 77
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: School Principal
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 70

In his mind, the rain still falls on that Tuesday. He walks from his car to the faculty entrance of Oakridge High, keys between his knuckles, when a man steps from behind the landscaping shed. Two hands seize his shoulders. A voice demands his wallet. Cold metal presses against his ribs. He hands over the leather pouch without argument. He walks away until he reaches the safety of his office, then calls his wife only when his hands stop shaking. In the present, the memory plays with the same clarity, the same sudden drop in his stomach. At seventy-seven, he has spent decades leading this campus. His wife of forty-two years knows he is different now. He starts each morning pacing the perimeter of their yard before the house wakes. He checks the deadbolt twice, then a third time. When he arrives at Oakridge, he no longer walks the main hallway. He takes the service corridor, eyes scanning over the shoulders of passing students, timing how long it takes for security to reach the east wing. Teachers notice the shift. He used to greet them by name, lean against doorframes, laugh at faculty meeting jokes. Now his greetings are tight, his posture rigid, his voice stripped of its usual warmth. He catches himself gripping the edge of his mahogany desk until his knuckles match the silver of his wedding band. At night, sleep fractures into fragments of running. He wakes gasping, the phantom weight of hands on his shoulders pressing down until the sheets feel like a trap. He rises anyway, makes tea he doesn’t drink, and watches the streetlights flicker past the blinds. His wife’s hand on his back sometimes makes him flinch. He hates that it does. He wonders if he is failing them all. He still signs the budgets. He still sits at the head of the table during discipline reviews. But the authority he once wore like a second skin now feels like borrowed armor. When a student raises their voice in the hallway, his pulse jumps to his throat. He tells himself it is merely a teenager being loud, but his body does not wait for that logic. He finds himself avoiding the parking garage entirely, taking the long way around the building, tracing the route he took that night over and over in his mind, rewriting the ending, searching for the moment he should have acted differently. He laughs less at lunch. He stops staying after school for parent conferences. His principal’s journal, once filled with lesson plans and community event details, now holds only fragmented notes: gate latch sticks, call maintenance, note camera blind spot near north stairs. In the quiet of this room, he speaks in measured paragraphs, each sentence carefully guarded. He describes the weight of carrying a school through funding cuts and staff turnover, the expectation that he should be unshakable. When I ask what happens when he sits in his office with the blinds drawn, he pauses. He looks at his hands, then at the floor. He says he waits. He waits for the phone to ring with news that everything is fine, that the threat was only memory, that the ground beneath him has not shifted without his permission. He listens to the hum of the HVAC system, counts the seconds between heartbeats, and wonders how long he can keep building a life on the assumption that the door will always lock from the inside.
